newsitem.title: USA: U.S. commends Europe over tougher Cuba line.
newsitem.headline: U.S. commends Europe over tougher Cuba line.

text.p: The United States on Monday commended the European Union for taking a tougher line on Cuba and hinted it could prompt the White House to go on waiving penalties against foreign firms that do business in Cuba.
"We welcome this important change from words to action by the European Union," the State Department said after the 15-nation grouping vowed to pressure communist-ruled Cuba to respect human rights.

"This new common position clearly demonstrates the EU's commitment to work in a more active, coordinated and sustained fashion toward the common goal of promoting a peaceful democratic transition in Cuba," a statement said.
Under the new strategy, the EU will seek opportunities of reminding the Cuban authorities of their "fundamental responsibilities on human rights, in particular freedom of speech and association."

Washington has been pushing the EU for months to adopt such an initiative, which has been promoted in several trips to Europe by Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, a former ambassador to the Union.

The United States and the EU are at loggerheads over this year's Helms-Burton law, which imposes penalties on foreign firms that use nationalised property in Cuba that formerly belonged to U.S. citizens.

In an attempt to soften the law, President Bill Clinton last July waived for six months a major provision allowing U.S. citizens to sue such companies in American courts. He must decide by Jan. 16 on a possible further six-month waiver.

Without specifically confirming a trade-off, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Monday's move by the EU "certainly will be a factor" in the decision, although he added there would be other factors.

"When the White House and the State Department discussed the president's and the government's views on Helms-Burton last summer, we did indicate at the time that we hoped that the Europeans would pay more attention to human rights in Cuba," Burns told a news briefing.

The only provision of Helms-Burton affecting foreigners that has been enforced is one banning top executives of companies that "traffick" in former U.S. property in Cuba from visiting the United States.
This has so far been applied only to Canada's Sherritt International Corp. and Mexico's Grupo Domos.

Washington's allies protest that Helms-Burton seeks to apply U.S. law beyond U.S. territory, and last month succeeded in getting the World Trade Organisation to establish a panel to study the validity of the legislation.

In a conciliatory statement, Burns said the United States recognised "that the EU's approach toward Cuba is different from our own, and that the EU will continue to act independently, as it has today".
"The United States is hopeful, however, that this approach will contribute to our objective of promoting democracy, freedom and respect for human rights in Cuba," he said.
"Today's action is a major step forward in showing that the human rights situation in Cuba is a priority concern, not just for those of us in our own hemisphere, but for the entire world," he added.

The Clinton administration originally opposed Helms-Burton, but swung round to supporting it after Cuban fighters last February shot down two light planes flown by Cuban exiles off the island's coast.
